narrative:
The model predicted a 64% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. The strongest influence came from your plan to attend part-time. Among accepted students, only 7% planned to work while studying, while the vast majority attended full-time. This choice strongly pushed the prediction toward failure, as part-time study is strongly associated with lower first-time bar passage rates.

Your first-year grades were the second most important factor. Placing in the fourth decile is noticeably below the average of sixth decile among accepted students, and this weaker early performance pushed the model toward expecting you to fail the bar.

Your third-year grades worked in the opposite direction. Ranking in the seventh decile—slightly above the accepted-student average—gave the model some confidence that your performance had improved and pulled the prediction back toward passing. However, this positive signal was not strong enough to overcome the other two factors.

Taken together, the combination of part-time attendance and relatively low first-year grades created enough concern about your likelihood of passing the bar that the school could not offer admission.

You should consider reapplying after improving your first-year academic record or switching to a full-time schedule if possible. Strengthening either of those areas would likely change the outcome in a future application. (248 words)
